title: Something before heaven
hook: something formed before heaven and earth; the Tao follows what is so of itself (Tao Te Ching 25)

segments.voice: Yesterday, chapter twenty-four, on tiptoe, and your line was flat feet. When did you catch yourself straining, and come back down? Day one thousand eighty-seven.

A plant on a kitchen windowsill. Nobody turned it. Nobody gave it instructions. But over a few weeks every leaf has swung around to face the glass, and the stems are leaning toward the light like people at a parade barrier. It didn't try. It didn't decide. It just did what a plant does. Turn it around and, given time, it will do it again. Chapter twenty-five of the Tao Te Ching reaches back before the world began, and then lands on something as ordinary as that plant: a thing being what it is.
screen: `A PLANT ON A WINDOWSILL.` → `NOBODY TURNED IT.` → `IT JUST DID WHAT IT DOES.`

segments.voice: First, something before heaven. In Legge's translation the chapter opens: "There was something undefined and complete, coming into existence before Heaven and Earth." Still, formless, standing alone, it says, not changing, going everywhere without wearing out. It could be called the mother of everything under heaven. Second, no name, so call it the Way. Then the speaker admits a problem. He doesn't know its name. So he calls it Tao, the Way, and if pushed for a name, he calls it great. And great, the chapter says, means it goes far out, and going far out, it comes back. Third, each takes its law from the next. Near the end comes a chain. People follow the earth. The earth follows heaven. Heaven follows the Way. You'd expect the chain to stop there, at the top. It doesn't. Fourth, the Way follows ziran. The last link, in Legge's words: "The law of the Tao is its being what it is." The Chinese word there is ziran. Translators render it as what is so of itself, or naturalness, or spontaneity. Not a higher power above the Way, but the Way simply being itself, the way the plant leans toward the window without being told. So the chapter climbs from people all the way past heaven, and at the very top finds no ruler at all, only something doing what it does. Some readers take this as a key to the whole book: the deepest thing isn't forced, and doesn't force.
screen: `SOMETHING BEFORE HEAVEN.` · `NO NAME, SO CALL IT THE WAY.` · `EACH TAKES ITS LAW FROM THE NEXT.` · `THE WAY FOLLOWS ZIRAN.` · then, large: `ITS BEING WHAT IT IS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch something grow, or move, on its own. Find something alive nearby: a plant, a tree out the window, your own breath. Settle, and just watch it. Don't help it, don't judge it. The plant isn't trying to grow. The breath isn't trying to breathe. Notice how much is happening with no effort from you at all. If your mind starts to manage, let it rest and go back to watching. The bell holds the time.
Ziran. What is so of itself: naturalness, the way a thing is when nothing is pushing it. In chapter twenty-five, it's what even the Way follows. Today's word.
Your line: so of itself. Today, let one thing happen at its own pace, a kettle, a conversation, a child getting dressed, without hurrying it along. Day one thousand eighty-seven.

howItsDone: In Taoist thought, ziran, being so of itself, is an ideal: some practitioners spend time in nature or in quiet watching to sense how things unfold without being forced.

original.note: Chinese, zìrán: so of itself, naturalness. In Tao Te Ching 25 the Way follows it.

trapdoor: what you thought: ziran is just the Chinese word for nature, the trees and rivers.
what it means: being so of itself, a thing being what it is with nothing pushing it.
what a scholar hears: the last link of chapter twenty-five's chain, people, earth, heaven, the Way, ziran, with no ruler above the Way.

notes: Verify both Legge 1891 quotations against the text.
Chapter 25's middle is paraphrased, including 'great means it goes far out, and going far out, it comes back' (大曰逝，逝曰遠，遠曰反, compressed). Confirm the compression is fair.
The chapter's mention of the king among the 'four great things' is left out for length.
Ziran is glossed as 'what is so of itself', 'naturalness' or 'spontaneity', attributed to translators; no etymology of the characters is claimed. Confirm.

In some readings 道法自然 means 'the Way models itself on what is so of itself', with ziran not a separate thing at all; the teach says 'not a higher power above the Way' to reflect that. Check the framing.
howItsDone calls ziran an ideal in Taoist thought; confirm.
'Some readers take this as a key to the whole book' is attributed, not asserted.
